title: The Rendezvous
summary: In Rome, the Count of Monte Cristo asks Albert to introduce him to Paris society, and they fix a precise appointment: 21 May, 10:30 a.m., at Albert's home. Franz, uneasy, tells Albert everything he knows about the Count, but Albert brushes his fears aside.
details: The morning after his rescue from the bandits, Albert de Morcerf, with Franz d'Épinay, goes to thank the Count of Monte Cristo again and offers the help of his family, including his father, the Comte de Morcerf, a man of Spanish origin with influence in Paris and Madrid. The Count accepts at once: he has never seen Paris, he says, and needs someone to open the doors of fashionable society to him. Albert mentions that his father has called him home to arrange a marriage.

The Count, insisting on his punctuality, sets the meeting three months ahead: the 21st of May at half-past ten in the morning, at Albert's rooms, No. 27 Rue du Helder. Franz watches him closely, remembering the plans the Count hinted at in the grotto of Monte Cristo. When they shake hands on parting, the Count's hand feels as cold as a corpse's.

Alone with Albert, Franz breaks his silence and tells him everything: the island, the smugglers and Corsican bandits, the enchanted underground palace, the hashish, the conversation he overheard at the Colosseum between the Count and Vampa, and how the Count freed Albert. Albert explains it all away. Rich men own yachts and take titles from land they buy, Corsican bandits are just outlaws, and in any case the Count saved his life and 4,000 piastres without asking a single question. Franz gives up the argument, though he still calls the Count a most singular man.
The next day the friends part, Albert for Paris and Franz for Venice. Before leaving, Albert leaves a card for the Count with the address and date written on it.

title: The Guests
summary: In Paris on the morning of 21 May, Albert prepares a breakfast for the Count in his elegant bachelor pavilion. His first guests arrive: Lucien Debray, a minister's private secretary, and Beauchamp, a newspaper editor.
details: The scene moves to Paris. Albert lives in a pavilion in the courtyard of his parents' grand house, the home of the Count and Countess of Morcerf, a place clearly chosen by a loving mother who wanted to keep her son close while giving him his freedom. The narrator describes his rooms in detail: a private side door, a smoking room stocked with every kind of tobacco, and a studio crammed with musical instruments, paintings, fencing gear, armor, antiques and stuffed birds, the remains of a string of passing hobbies.

At a quarter to ten his valet Germain brings the post. Albert accepts a seat in Madame Danglars' opera box and asks for a liqueur set from his mother, telling her he will introduce someone to her that afternoon. He admits he does not fully trust the Count to keep the appointment, but means to be punctual himself.

Lucien Debray arrives first, a cool, fashionable young man who is private secretary to the Minister of the Interior. He has been up all night writing dispatches about Spanish affairs, and mentions that the banker M. Danglars somehow learned the news early and made a million on the stock exchange. He also says he dined the night before at M. de Villefort's. Beauchamp, a journalist on an opposition paper, comes next, and the two trade friendly political insults while Albert waits for his last two guests.

title: The Breakfast
summary: Château-Renaud arrives with Captain Maximilian Morrel, who saved his life in Algeria. As the clock strikes half-past ten the Count of Monte Cristo appears, dazzles the company, reacts with visible emotion to Morrel, and reveals he already has a house in Paris.
details: While they wait, the guests gossip about Albert's expected engagement to Eugénie Danglars, daughter of the newly made Baron Danglars. Château-Renaud, a nobleman of old family, arrives with Maximilian Morrel, a captain of Spahis (French cavalry in Algeria). Morrel saved Château-Renaud from Arab horsemen on the 5th of September, a date he honors each year as the anniversary of the day his father was miraculously saved. Albert then tells his own story of being kidnapped in Rome and set free by the Count of Monte Cristo. The others laugh at it, though Morrel remarks that Monte Cristo is a small island he has heard old sailors such as Penelon talk about.

On the stroke of half-past ten the Count enters without a sound. He greets everyone politely and coolly, but at Morrel's name he steps forward and colors, and his voice trembles as he praises Morrel's noble heart. At table he eats little, shows off an emerald box of opium-and-hashish pills, mentions gifts of emeralds to the Sultan and the Pope, explains how he once captured Vampa and let him go, and declares he protects no society that does not protect him.

The Count says he has a credit with Baron Danglars through several banks, among them Thomson & French of Rome. Morrel starts at that name: this firm once did his family a great service and has always denied it. Each guest suggests a district for the Count to live in, and Morrel offers rooms at his sister Julie's house, where she lives happily with her husband Emmanuel Herbaut. The Count declines. His mute Nubian servant Ali has already bought and furnished a house on the Champs-Élysées, his steward Bertuccio has taken boxes at the theatres, and he mentions a Greek slave. Morrel leaves his card, and the Count promises to visit.

title: The Presentation
summary: Albert shows the Count his rooms and introduces him to his parents. The Count goes pale before a portrait of Albert's mother in Catalan dress; the Countess is Mercédès. Afterwards she questions Albert anxiously about the Count and warns him to be careful.
details: Albert takes the Count around his rooms and finds that his guest knows the date and origin of every object and the painter of every picture. In the bedroom the Count stops dead before a portrait of a dark-eyed young woman in the dress of a Catalan fisherwoman, gazing at the sea. He turns pale and breathes hard, then calmly calls her a charming mistress. Albert explains that it is his mother. His father dislikes the portrait, and his mother rarely looks at it without crying.

In the main house the Count admires the Morcerf coat of arms with hidden irony and meets the Count of Morcerf, a general and peer of France who looks older than his years and whose worn face seems to the Count to tell a story of secret troubles. Morcerf explains that he left the army after the July Revolution of 1830 and went into politics. The Count flatters him lavishly. Then the Countess appears in the doorway, pale and motionless. The narrator names her: Mercédès. She thanks the Count for saving her son, and he, even paler than she is, bows deeply. He declines her invitation to stay and leaves in a splendid new carriage, noticing as he goes that the curtain of her window moves.

Albert finds his mother lying in a darkened room, smelling salts beside her, blaming the strong scent of the flowers. She asks whether Monte Cristo is a real name, how old the Count is (thirty-five, Albert thinks, which seems to shock her), and whether he is really what he appears to be. She urges Albert to be prudent, then asks how his father received the guest. Albert thinks she has fallen asleep and tiptoes out, concluding that if his mother noticed the Count, he must be remarkable.

title: Monsieur Bertuccio
summary: At his new house on the Champs-Élysées, the Count buys a country house at Auteuil without looking at it. His steward Bertuccio turns pale at the address, and the Count insists that Bertuccio come with him to see it that same evening.
details: The Count arrives at the house Ali has chosen for him on the Champs-Élysées, where Ali and his steward Bertuccio are waiting. Bertuccio reports that the Count's new visiting cards have been engraved and the first one taken to Baron Danglars. A notary is waiting to complete the sale of a country house the Count wants to buy.

The Count claims not to know where the house is. When the notary says Auteuil, just outside Paris, Bertuccio goes pale and suggests several better places instead. The Count signs anyway, pays more than the asking price, and sends the delighted notary away.

Alone, the Count unlocks a private notebook he keeps on a key round his neck and checks the address in the deed against his notes: 'Auteuil, Rue de la Fontaine, No. 28; it is indeed the same.' He wonders aloud whether he can trust a confession 'extorted by religious or physical terror', and says that within an hour he will know everything. He then asks Bertuccio whether he knows the area around Paris. Bertuccio, trembling, says no, and is horrified to learn that he must come to Auteuil at once. The steward, who has never dared to disobey, follows his master into the carriage.

title: The House at Auteuil
summary: At the Auteuil house, which once belonged to the Marquis de Saint-Méran, the terrified Bertuccio admits that he committed a killing in its garden as an act of revenge, and that his victim was M. de Villefort.
details: Bertuccio crosses himself in the Corsican way and grows more frightened as they drive into Auteuil. The caretaker tells them the house's former owner was the Marquis de Saint-Méran, a loyal Bourbon supporter whose only daughter married M. de Villefort, once the king's attorney at Nîmes, and died twenty-one years ago. Bertuccio has to lean on the wall to stay upright.

The Count makes Bertuccio light the way through the house and down a private staircase into the garden. There Bertuccio freezes and begs his master to move away from a certain spot, the place where 'he fell'. The Count coldly threatens to send him to an asylum or dismiss him. He reminds Bertuccio that he came to him with a letter of recommendation from the Abbé Busoni, who heard his confession in prison at Nîmes, and he says he will hold the abbé responsible.

Desperate not to lose his position, Bertuccio admits that he committed a vendetta (a Corsican blood revenge) in this very garden, and that two steps from the spot is the grave in which the victim had just buried his child. He says the Count, standing in his cloak under the plane tree, reminds him of the man: M. de Villefort, the magistrate with the spotless reputation, who was, Bertuccio says, a villain. The Count sits down on a bench, humming an opera tune, and orders him to tell the whole story.

title: The Vendetta
summary: Bertuccio tells his story: Villefort refused justice for his murdered brother, so he declared a vendetta, stabbed Villefort in the Auteuil garden, and saved the baby Villefort was burying. Years later, hiding at Caderousse's inn, he watched Caderousse sell the abbé's diamond to a jeweller.
details: In 1815 Bertuccio's elder brother, a Corsican officer of Napoleon's army, was murdered in Nîmes during the royalist massacres. Bertuccio begged the king's attorney there, Villefort, to find the killers and to grant the widow, Assunta, a pension. Villefort dismissed the dead man as a soldier of 'the usurper' and threatened to throw Bertuccio out, so Bertuccio declared a vendetta against him. He followed Villefort to Versailles and discovered his secret visits to the Auteuil house, where a young, pregnant woman known only as 'the Baroness' was living.

One stormy September night Bertuccio hid in the garden and saw Villefort come out with a spade and bury a box. He stabbed him and dug up the box, thinking it held treasure. Inside was a newborn baby, nearly suffocated. Bertuccio revived it and left it at the foundling hospital in Paris, keeping half of its linen, which was marked with an H and an N under a baron's coronet. Assunta later reclaimed the boy and named him Benedetto. He grew up charming but wicked, stealing and lying, and once taunted Bertuccio that he was not his father.

In June 1829, while running from customs officers, Bertuccio hid in a shed beside Gaspard Caderousse's inn on the Beaucaire road. Through the wall he watched Caderousse and his wife, La Carconte, sell a diamond to a Paris jeweller named Joannes. It had been left to them, they said, by a sailor named Edmond Dantès and delivered by an Abbé Busoni. The jeweller paid 45,000 francs and set off into a storm, ignoring the couple's greedy whispers. Then a knock came: Joannes was back, asking to spend the night.

title: The Rain of Blood
summary: Bertuccio finishes his tale: the Caderousses murdered the jeweller, Caderousse fled, and Bertuccio was arrested for the crime until the Abbé Busoni came to his aid. Benedetto later tortured Assunta for money and vanished. That night Haydée arrives at the Count's Paris house.
details: La Carconte fawned over the jeweller and put him to bed. Bertuccio dozed off and woke to a pistol shot, screams and a struggle overhead, and warm drops falling on his face through the floor. Caderousse came down covered in blood, took the diamond and the money, and fled. Bertuccio broke through to help and found La Carconte shot dead on the stairs and Joannes dying of knife wounds. Customs officers and gendarmes burst in, found Bertuccio soaked in blood, and arrested him.

In prison at Nîmes he begged the authorities to find the Abbé Busoni. After three months the abbé appeared, confirmed the diamond story, and heard Bertuccio's confession, including the Auteuil killing. Caderousse was later caught, confessed, and was sent to the galleys for life, and Bertuccio was freed. The abbé then recommended him to the Count. Back in Corsica, Bertuccio found that Benedetto and two companions had held Assunta over a fire to make her reveal where her money was hidden, then robbed the house and disappeared. She died of her burns. 'Those Villeforts are an accursed race,' Bertuccio says, and the Count murmurs agreement.

The Count tells him that his real crime was not returning the rescued baby to its mother, and that the wicked are not so easily gone: Benedetto may be alive. He sends Bertuccio away, studies the garden as a 'plan' laid out before him, and murmurs that the prosecutor may not be dead. Back on the Champs-Élysées, he moves through the house as if he has always known it, and at midnight welcomes Haydée, the beautiful young Greek woman from Italy, to her secret apartments.

title: Unlimited Credit
summary: Baron Danglars calls at the Count's house and is turned away. The Count has Danglars' prized horses bought out from under him, then visits the banker and crushes his doubts about an 'unlimited' credit, arranging to draw six million francs in the first year.
details: Baron Danglars, a showy, sly-looking man past fifty with dyed hair, drives up and is told the Count is not receiving. From behind his blinds the Count studies him through a lorgnette and remarks on his 'decidedly bad countenance'. He orders Bertuccio to buy Danglars' fine horses at double the price, and reassures the anxious Ali kindly in Arabic. He tells his valet Baptistin that he must never gossip about his master, and adds that he keeps a fund for loyal servants. Ali, he says, is not a servant but a slave whose life is his. He also orders Bertuccio to find him an estate on the Normandy coast with a harbor for his corvette, and to keep his ships and relays of horses ready.

At five o'clock the Count drives to Danglars' house in the Chaussée d'Antin behind the banker's own horses. Danglars has just told his colleagues he suspects a hoax: Thomson & French of Rome have given this so-called count unlimited credit with him. In his gaudy white-and-gold drawing room he tries to patronize the Count, who mocks his titles. When Danglars grandly offers 'even a million', the Count pulls two treasury notes of 500,000 francs each from his card case and shows further letters of unlimited credit on Rothschild and Lafitte.

Danglars is overwhelmed. They settle on six million francs for the year, beginning with 500,000 the next morning. The Count says his fortune is an old family treasure only recently released to him, and adds, with a ghastly smile, that Danglars will soon know more about him. Danglars offers to present him to the Baroness, who is with Lucien Debray. The Count smiles, since he already knows the banker's domestic secrets.

title: The Dappled Grays
summary: Madame Danglars is furious that her husband sold her dappled grays, now pulling the Count's carriage. The Count returns them decorated with diamonds. Next day the horses bolt at Auteuil with Madame de Villefort and her son aboard, and Ali stops them.
details: The Count is presented to Madame Danglars in her pink boudoir, where Debray is also present. She has heard all about the Count from Debray and Albert. Her maid then reports that her pair of dappled gray horses, promised for Madame de Villefort's drive the next day, have vanished from the stable. Danglars stammers excuses and whispers that he sold them at a huge profit, just as Debray spots the grays harnessed to the Count's carriage outside. Debray slips away before the quarrel breaks out, and the Count leaves pleased: 'The domestic peace of this family is henceforth in my hands.' Two hours later he sends the horses back with a large diamond fixed in each rosette of their harness.

At Auteuil the next day the Count asks Ali whether his lasso could stop two runaway horses, and stations him outside the house. At five o'clock the grays come racing by, out of control, carrying a young woman and a small boy. Ali lassoes one horse and grips the other by the nostrils. The Count carries the pair inside and revives the unconscious boy with a single drop of a blood-red elixir.

The lady is Héloïse de Villefort, wife of the king's attorney, and the boy is her spoiled son Edward, who goes straight for the Count's bottles of drugs and calls Ali 'too ugly' to thank. The Count warns that some of the liquids are dangerous even to smell, and notices her glance at the case. Ali drives them home behind the now sluggish horses. She writes to her friend Hermine Danglars, begging to meet the Count again, and all Paris talks of the adventure. That night M. de Villefort, in full dress, calls at the Count's house.

title: Ideology
summary: Villefort, now a cold, powerful royal prosecutor in Paris, comes to thank the Count. They spar about justice: the Count calls himself an agent of Providence sent to reward and punish, and Villefort answers with the story of his father Noirtier, struck down by paralysis.
details: The narrator describes M. de Villefort as he is now. He is a respected and much-feared king's attorney who has survived four revolutions, rarely pays visits, runs a stiff, correct household with his young wife and his daughter by his first marriage, and despises dreamers and theories. He has grown thin and yellow, wears gold spectacles and dresses all in black. He arrives suspecting the Count is an adventurer or an escaped criminal.

The Count meets his stiff thanks with a chilly reply and then a string of provocations. He has studied the laws of every nation and found the primitive law of retaliation closest to God's law. There are men, he says, whom God sends with a mission rather than a post, and he is one of them, a man of no country, stopped only by death. Asked his ambition, he tells a parable: Satan offered him the world, and he answered that he wished to be Providence, because nothing is finer than to reward and punish. He was made one of Providence's agents, and would make the same bargain again. He adds that he has been 'nearly mad' once.

Shaken, Villefort warns him that worse things than death exist, such as apoplexy (a stroke). He describes his father, M. Noirtier, once a fearless Jacobin and Bonapartist plotter, now paralyzed and speechless overnight and dependent on his granddaughter Valentine. Villefort calls this God's punishment of his father alone, while his children Valentine and Edward are his compensation. The Count smiles while groaning inwardly, promises to visit, and, once Villefort leaves, says: 'Enough of this poison, let me now seek the antidote.'

title: Haydée
summary: Before visiting the Morrels, the Count spends an hour with Haydée in her Eastern apartments. He tells her she is free in France and may leave him; she insists she will never leave him. He asks her to keep the secret of her birth.
details: After Villefort's visit the Count looks forward to calling on old friends in the Rue Meslay: Maximilian, Julie and Emmanuel. To prepare himself, he first spends an hour with Haydée. She lives in rooms furnished in Eastern style, with Turkish carpets and silk divans, and has three French maids and a Greek one, all ordered to treat her like a queen. The narrator describes her: about nineteen or twenty, dressed in the costume of Epirus (a region of north-western Greece), smoking a narghile (water pipe), strikingly beautiful.

She greets him in Greek, asking why he asks permission to enter when he is her master. The Count tells her that in France she is free, free even to leave him, and that she may find someone she prefers. Haydée answers that she has loved no one but him and her father, and that her love for him is not a daughter's love: if he died, she would die too.

He gives her full freedom of the house, a carriage, and Ali and her maid Myrtho to go with her. He asks only one thing: that she keep the secret of her birth and never speak the names of her 'illustrious father' or 'ill-fated mother'. He then leaves for the Morrels', murmuring lines of Pindar about youth and love.

title: The Morrel Family
summary: The Count visits Maximilian, Julie and Emmanuel, whose happiness moves him deeply. They show him relics of their unknown benefactor, 'Sinbad the Sailor'. He suggests a 'Lord Wilmore', then leaves abruptly on hearing old Morrel died believing their rescuer was Edmond Dantès.
details: The Morrels' house in the Rue Meslay is cheerful and comfortable. The one-eyed Cocles, now the doorkeeper, does not recognize the Count, and the old sailor Penelon is the gardener. Maximilian explains that his father died leaving 500,000 francs. Julie and her husband Emmanuel worked until they had earned 250,000 francs more, then closed the firm rather than risk the Morrel name, and now live happily on a modest income.

The Count is so moved by their contentment that he can barely speak. Julie says that God once sent them an angel. Under a glass cover they keep their dearest treasures: a silk purse, a letter signed 'Sinbad the Sailor', and the diamond given to Julie as her dowry. These are relics of the stranger who saved their father from suicide and the firm from ruin. They have never been able to thank him. Penelon once glimpsed the Englishman who visited in 1829, a clerk from Thomson & French, boarding a yacht at Trieste.

The Count, uneasy under Julie's gaze, describes the Englishman exactly, then claims he must have been a friend of his, an eccentric Lord Wilmore who did such kindnesses secretly and did not believe in gratitude. He says Wilmore has left for distant lands and will never return. Maximilian adds that their father always said 'It was no Englishman', and that his last words were 'Maximilian, it was Edmond Dantès!' The Count goes deathly pale, makes hurried excuses and leaves. Julie says his voice seemed familiar.

title: Pyramus and Thisbe
summary: Maximilian Morrel and Valentine de Villefort, secretly in love, meet at a boarded-up gate in her family's garden. Valentine, unhappily engaged to Franz d'Épinay, describes her lonely home life and odd reactions to Morrel's name. The Count's arrival interrupts them.
details: Behind a grand house in the Faubourg Saint-Honoré, a disused gate separates the garden from an abandoned vegetable plot. Here a young woman waits by the planks, and a tall young man in a workman's blouse slips in to meet her: Maximilian Morrel and Valentine de Villefort. (The chapter takes its title from Pyramus and Thisbe, lovers in an old legend who talked through a crack in a wall.) To meet her safely, Maximilian has rented the plot as a 'gardener' for 500 francs a year.

Valentine is afraid. She is engaged to Franz d'Épinay, and her father never changes his mind. At home she feels like an outcast: her father ignores her, and her stepmother hates her behind constant smiles, perhaps because Valentine has her own mother's fortune and will inherit from her grandparents, the Saint-Mérans, while Madame de Villefort's adored son Edward has nothing. Her only comfort is her paralyzed grandfather Noirtier, who can speak only with his eyes. Maximilian promises patience: Franz is not due back for a year.

Valentine asks whether their fathers ever quarrelled in Marseilles. When she read aloud the news of Maximilian's promotion in the Legion of Honor, her father started and sneered at the Bonapartist Morrels of 1815, and she thought M. Danglars, who was present, trembled too. Noirtier, however, signalled with his eyes that he was glad of Maximilian's honor. A maid then calls Valentine indoors: the Count of Monte Cristo has come to call. Maximilian wonders how the Count knows M. de Villefort.

title: Toxicology
summary: The Count calls on Madame de Villefort and reminds her that they once discussed poisons at Perugia. She eagerly draws him out on how poisons can kill without leaving traces, and he gives her a dangerous elixir, pleased that 'the seed sown' has found fertile soil.
details: Villefort is out, so Madame de Villefort receives the Count with Edward, who torments a parrot and tears up an album while his mother barely scolds him. Valentine comes in, sad and recently in tears. The Count claims to remember them all from Perugia two years earlier, and Madame de Villefort finally recalls talking at length with a man in a long cloak she took for a doctor. They had discussed the famous aqua Tofana, a legendary Italian poison, and she had asked about Valentine's health. At six o'clock she sends Valentine off to give Noirtier his dinner and sends Edward after her, closing the door carefully.

Alone with the Count, she returns again and again to poison. The Count explains how Mithridates, an ancient king, made himself immune by taking small, increasing doses; how Eastern poisoners cover their tracks; and how a 'terrible chemist' he knew, the Abbé Adelmonte, poisoned a cabbage with strychnine so that, passed along a chain of animals, it left no trace except what looked like apoplexy (a stroke). She shows that she already knows a good deal of chemistry. When she raises conscience, he answers with cases of people who excused their crimes as acts of love, among them Lady Macbeth, who he says wanted a throne for her son.

She asks about the elixir that revived Edward. One drop restores life, he says, while five or six would kill and could not be tasted in a glass of wine. He offers her the recipe and leaves for the opera. She thinks he must be the Adelmonte he talks about. The Count, satisfied, reflects that 'this is a fruitful soil', and sends the prescription the next morning.

title: Robert le Diable
summary: At the opera, all Paris stares at the Count and Haydée. In Madame Danglars' box the Count meets Eugénie and the Count of Morcerf, who served Ali Pasha at Yanina. Seeing Morcerf, Haydée nearly faints: this man, she says, sold her father to the Turks.
details: At a performance of Meyerbeer's opera Robert le Diable, Albert and Château-Renaud chat loudly in the stalls. A mystery horse entered as 'Vampa' has won the Jockey Club cup, and the Countess G——, the lovely Venetian from Rome, has received the cup 'from Lord Ruthven', the vampire nickname she once gave the Count. Albert visits her and confirms that it was the Count. Madame Danglars arrives escorted by Debray (openly hinted to be her lover) with her daughter Eugénie: handsome, cold and strong-willed, gifted in music and languages, who studies with a poor young singer, Louise d'Armilly. Albert finds her beauty too severe for his taste.

The Count enters a box with Haydée, whose beauty and diamonds hold everyone's attention. In Madame Danglars' box the ladies quiz Albert about the Count. Albert then meets the Count in the corridor, who asks whether the Count of Morcerf ever comes to the opera. Later the Count visits the baroness's box, where Morcerf has now arrived. Eugénie coolly asks whether Haydée is his daughter. Madame Danglars mentions that Morcerf served Ali Tepelini, and Morcerf confirms he was inspector-general of the Pasha's troops at Yanina and owes his fortune to him.

The Count leans over the front of the box with his arm around Morcerf, just as Haydée looks across. She sees Morcerf's face next to her guardian's, cries out and falls back in her seat. The Count excuses her nerves and returns to her. Trembling, she calls Morcerf a wretch: 'he sold my father to the Turks, and the fortune he boasts of was the price of his treachery!' The Count says he heard something of this in Epirus and asks her to tell him the details some day. They leave as the fourth act begins.

title: A Flurry in Stocks
summary: Albert confides that he dreads marrying Eugénie Danglars, a match his mother opposes. Debray squirms at a joke about tricking Madame Danglars on the stock market. The Count plans an Auteuil dinner without the Morcerfs and expects Major Cavalcanti and his son Andrea.
details: Albert and Debray call on the Count. Albert explains that his father and Danglars made their fortunes in Spain, his father in the army and Danglars supplying it. He does not love Eugénie, and his mother, for reasons he cannot explain, strongly dislikes the match with the Danglars family. Albert faked an illness to delay a meeting, but the two-month postponement ends next week.

Debray works out how much Danglars made on Haitian bonds, and lets slip that it is really Madame Danglars who gambles on the stock exchange. Albert jokes that Debray, who receives government news before anyone else, should teach her a lesson by feeding her a false report so she loses money. Debray is visibly embarrassed. The Count notices it, says something quietly to Debray as he leaves, and Debray replies, 'Willingly, count; I accept.'

The Count plans a dinner at Auteuil on Saturday for the Danglars and Villefort families. He tactfully leaves out the Morcerfs so that the Countess will not see it as a marriage meeting, and Albert decides to take his mother to the seaside at Tréport. The Count declines Albert's invitation to dine with his mother: he is expecting Major Bartolomeo Cavalcanti, an Italian nobleman, and his son Andrea, a young man making his entry into Paris society with his father's millions, whom the Count has promised to look after. Albert jokingly suggests finding Andrea a rich wife such as Eugénie. He also mentions that Franz is to marry Valentine de Villefort, and that Franz's father, General d'Épinay, was assassinated in 1815 by Bonapartists. Finally the Count orders Bertuccio to redecorate the Auteuil house, but to leave the red damask bedroom and the garden exactly as they are.
